items.title: Dave Rivello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012
items.q: The term 'Dorian' is mentioned by the interviewer as a musical scale/concept ('I don’t think Dorian. Why should I think Dorian?'), not as a person. The interviewee responds to the theoretical question about the scale.

ctx.x: Yeah, it’s true. But if it’s that important it’s that important. And I know I’ve kind of lost where your question was but I’ll get back there if I remember. But for me too I tell people that I could play an example I guess. Let’s see if I could make one up. I could spend hours trying to decide, is it this [piano chord] or is it this [piano chord]. Is it this [piano chord] I’ll play it a little better, or this [piano chord]. Oh I’m sure it’s this one [piano chord]. Well wait a minute, no, I think it’s this one…

Well maybe you answered my question but I think it’s partly that a person with that commitment may be the one that rises to the top. I mean there’s so many people out there now trying to get to the same spot, that it requires that kind of thing. I guess my question is, there’s so many names, there’s all the modes and there’s symmetric diminished and © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
there’s all these scales. And if I look at a Dm7 chord, I think of it as a major scale with a lowered third and a lowered seventh. I don’t think Dorian. Why should I think Dorian?
